# LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications

Keshu Wu Affiliation: Texas A&M University Affiliation: University of
Wisconsin-Madison    Hao Zhang Affiliation: Texas A&M University    Rui
Gan Affiliation: University of Wisconsin-Madison    Pei Li
Affiliation: University of Wyoming\[8pt\]    Jiwan Jiang
Affiliation: Texas A&M University    Yang Zhou Affiliation: Texas A&M
University

###### Abstract

Vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communication enables connected vehicles to
make safety-critical decisions, but delayed, missing, or incorrect
information can compromise driving safety. Systematically testing such
failures is challenging because traffic interactions, communication
conditions, and application responses must be jointly configured to
produce meaningful scenarios. This paper presents LAST-V2X, a
language-driven, adaptive framework for automated scenario synthesis and
safety testing of V2X applications. LAST-V2X leverages large language
models (LLMs) to translate natural-language test descriptions into
executable scenarios grounded in roadway geometry, V2X communication
semantics, and vehicle behavior. The framework integrates physical
traffic simulation with spatially aware communication modeling and
message-level fault injection to evaluate how information degradation
affects vehicle decisions. To establish whether an observed safety
failure is caused by communication rather than the underlying traffic
conditions, LAST-V2X employs matched executions under degraded and
ground-truth information. Furthermore, an execution-guided refinement
mechanism combines parameter search and LLM self-reflection to identify
ineffective test configurations, improve scenario effectiveness, and
produce minimal reproducible failure cases. Experiments across diverse
CARLA environments and V2X safety applications demonstrate the
framework’s ability to generate reliable scenarios, distinguish
communication-induced failures from unrelated safety violations, and
substantially improve failure discovery through adaptive refinement.
These results establish LAST-V2X as a systematic approach to
language-driven, causally verified, and adaptive safety testing for
connected vehicle systems.

## 1 Introduction

Vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communication extends a vehicle’s awareness
beyond onboard sensors \[[1](#bib.bib29), [2](#bib.bib30),
[3](#bib.bib31), [4](#bib.bib11), [5](#bib.bib64)\]. Roadside units
(RSUs) broadcast Signal Phase and Timing (SPaT) and intersection
geometry (MAP) messages, while connected vehicles exchange Basic Safety
Messages (BSMs). Applications such as Red-Light Violation Warning
(RLVW), Intersection Movement Assist (IMA), and Left Turn Assist (LTA)
use this information to support safety-critical decisions
\[[6](#bib.bib26), [7](#bib.bib13), [8](#bib.bib14)\]. This
communication–driving coupling also creates a cyber–physical safety
pathway: delayed, missing, or incorrect V2X information can alter
vehicle decisions and ultimately compromise safety. Systematically
testing such communication-induced failures is therefore increasingly
important. Constructing these tests manually is difficult because a
meaningful V2X scenario must coordinate roadway, traffic, vehicle
behavior, message type, communication condition, and fault timing. These
elements are strongly coupled: a delayed SPaT message, for example,
matters only when it occurs at the right movement, phase transition, and
decision time. The resulting scenario space is large and highly
structured, and many seemingly reasonable combinations are infeasible or
ineffective.

Beyond the difficulty of specifying coupled V2X scenarios, constructing
them in high-fidelity simulators can itself require substantial effort
to understand simulator APIs, scenario logic, traffic control, and
communication interfaces. Large language models (LLMs)
\[[9](#bib.bib28), [10](#bib.bib12)\] offer a natural bridge between
engineers’ high-level safety intents and the complex simulation logic
required to instantiate executable V2X test scenarios. Transportation
engineers can naturally express safety concerns in language. An LLM can
translate such intent into structured requirements, identify the
relevant safety application, connect semantic traffic roles with domain
concepts, and retrieve the roadway, communication, and behavioral
knowledge needed to instantiate the test \[[11](#bib.bib8),
[12](#bib.bib7), [13](#bib.bib62), [14](#bib.bib63), [15](#bib.bib65)\].
Recent language-driven methods have demonstrated the potential of
compiling natural-language descriptions into executable driving scenes
\[[16](#bib.bib6), [17](#bib.bib1), [18](#bib.bib4), [19](#bib.bib2),
[20](#bib.bib24), [21](#bib.bib37), [22](#bib.bib39), [23](#bib.bib48),
[24](#bib.bib53), [25](#bib.bib56), [26](#bib.bib57)\], a direction
recently surveyed in \[[27](#bib.bib54)\]. This capability is
particularly valuable for V2X, where a scenario depends not only on _how
vehicles move_, but also on _what information they exchange and what
each vehicle believes about the traffic state_. LLMs can therefore
reduce both scenario-engineering effort and simulator-programming burden
by orchestrating heterogeneous transportation, communication, and
simulation knowledge.

Despite this promise, generating a plausible V2X scenario does not
guarantee a meaningful safety test. A communication fault matters only
if it changes the information used by the V2X application and, in turn,
alters the vehicle’s physical behavior or safety outcome. This
cyber–physical effect can be difficult to establish because
communication failures take different forms, including packet loss,
latency, timestamp errors, decoding delays, frozen controller messages,
position errors, and incorrect lane-to-signal-group associations
\[[28](#bib.bib9), [29](#bib.bib10), [30](#bib.bib16), [31](#bib.bib25),
[32](#bib.bib41)\]. Some missing or delayed messages become stale and
can be detected by the application, potentially triggering a safe
fallback. In contrast, incorrect information may still appear fresh and
therefore be trusted, leading the vehicle to act on a wrong traffic
state. Safety-critical information may also be absent entirely, for
example when a conflicting vehicle does not transmit V2X messages.
Therefore, language-driven generation alone is insufficient: the
generated scenario must explicitly model how communication faults affect
application decisions and verify whether those effects actually
propagate into physical safety consequences.

Existing safety-critical scenario-generation methods primarily create
risk by modifying the _physical world_ \[[33](#bib.bib19),
[34](#bib.bib20), [35](#bib.bib34), [36](#bib.bib33), [37](#bib.bib49),
[38](#bib.bib55)\]: vehicle trajectories, behaviors, road conditions, or
initial states are perturbed until an unsafe interaction emerges
\[[39](#bib.bib17), [40](#bib.bib18), [41](#bib.bib3),
[42](#bib.bib5)\]. Recent language-driven approaches further allow such
physical scenarios to be specified and generated from natural-language
descriptions \[[17](#bib.bib1), [20](#bib.bib24), [43](#bib.bib32),
[44](#bib.bib36), [45](#bib.bib38), [46](#bib.bib35), [47](#bib.bib51),
[48](#bib.bib52), [49](#bib.bib58), [50](#bib.bib59), [51](#bib.bib60),
[52](#bib.bib61)\]. V2X safety testing, however, poses a fundamentally
different problem. The physical traffic scene may remain unchanged while
communication causes the ego vehicle to perceive a different state of
that scene. A signal may physically turn red while the received SPaT
still indicates green; a conflicting vehicle may physically exist while
its BSM is missing; or the roadway geometry may be correct while the
received MAP associates the ego with the wrong movement. The
safety-critical condition therefore arises not simply from _what happens
in the physical world_, but from a mismatch between the physical world
and the information available to the vehicle.

V2X co-simulation and digital-twin platforms provide mechanisms for
modeling message exchange, latency, packet loss, and
communication-dependent vehicle control \[[53](#bib.bib21),
[54](#bib.bib22), [55](#bib.bib23), [56](#bib.bib15), [29](#bib.bib10),
[57](#bib.bib42), [58](#bib.bib43)\]. Automated testing of V2X systems
has so far focused mainly on cooperative perception, for example by
transforming shared sensor data under varied communication and weather
conditions \[[59](#bib.bib40)\], rather than on message-level faults in
closed-loop safety applications. However, communication simulation alone
does not solve the testing problem. The physical interaction, message
semantics, fault type, fault timing, and application response must be
jointly constructed so that the information mismatch occurs precisely
when it can affect a safety-critical decision. A generated test may also
be executable yet ineffective because the selected fault is mistimed,
too weak, or semantically inconsistent with the intended failure
mechanism. Existing language-driven methods largely stop after scenario
generation or, when they close the loop, refine only the physical
adversarial behavior \[[46](#bib.bib35)\], while communication
simulators typically assume that the scenario and fault configuration
are already specified; neither provides a mechanism to use execution
evidence to diagnose why a test failed and revise the underlying test
intent. Moreover, observing a collision after injecting a communication
fault is insufficient to establish a V2X-induced failure, because the
same collision may occur even under healthy communication. Existing
language-driven scenario generation, communication simulation, and
safety falsification therefore address different parts of the problem,
but do not provide an integrated, self-refining framework for
constructing, diagnosing, refining, and causally validating failures
that originate in the information layer and propagate into the physical
world. This leads to the central question of this work: _can
natural-language V2X test intents be transformed into executable
scenarios that systematically expose and causally verify
communication-induced safety failures?_

![Refer to caption](2610.30979v1/framework_architecture.png)

Figure 1: Overview of LAST-V2X. _LLM Agent Analysis_ verifies the
intent; _Retrieval-Augmented Scenario Grounding_ places it on a feasible
junction; _Automated V2X Scenario Synthesis_ runs it in CARLA with
faulted messages beside a ground-truth ego; _Scenario Refinement_ admits
a failure only if the message-driven ego alone fails, else refines it.

To address this question, we develop LAST-V2X, an LLM-orchestrated
framework for communication-aware V2X safety testing. LAST-V2X first
converts natural-language intents into grounded scenario specifications,
then executes coupled traffic–communication scenarios in CARLA under
matched degraded and non-degraded communication conditions. Execution
evidence is further used to refine ineffective scenarios through
parameter search and LLM self-reflection, while successful failures are
reduced to minimal reproducible cases.

The main contributions are:

1.  1.  Coupled physical–information scenario generation. LAST-V2X jointly
        constructs the physical traffic scene and the V2X information
        perceived by the vehicle, with feasibility checks to reject
        ineffective tests before simulation.
2.  2.  Causal verification of communication-induced safety failures.
        Matched degraded and non-degraded executions determine whether V2X
        faults actually cause changes in physical safety outcomes.
3.  3.  Execution-grounded adaptive refinement. Parameter search corrects
        quantitative deficiencies, while LLM self-reflection revises
        semantically ineffective test intents using simulation evidence.
        Successful cases are further reduced to minimal reproducible
        failures.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
Section [2](#S2 "2 Methodology ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications")
formulates the testing problem and introduces the four modules of
LAST-V2X.
Section [3](#S3 "3 Experimental Results ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications")
presents the experimental evaluation, and
Section [4](#S4 "4 Conclusion ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications")
concludes the paper.

## 2 Methodology

As illustrated in
Fig. [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications"),
LAST-V2X contains four interdependent modules. _LLM Agent Analysis_
converts the user intent into a typed and feasibility-verified test
specification. _Retrieval-Augmented Scenario Grounding_ binds the
symbolic specification to roadway geometry, V2X domain knowledge, and
executable agent behaviors. _Automated V2X Scenario Synthesis_ realizes
the resulting program as a coupled physical–information simulation with
spatial communication, semantic message faults, and paired ego rollouts.
Finally, _Scenario Refinement_ uses execution evidence to search for,
diagnose, and minimize communication-induced failures. We first
formalize the problem solved by these four modules.

### 2.1 Problem Description

#### Scenario Specification

The input to LAST-V2X is a short free-form natural-language prompt $`p`$
describing a traffic situation to be tested. The prompt may specify the
environment, ego maneuver, surrounding vehicles, safety-critical
interaction, and optionally a communication condition or fault. A
compiler $`\mathcal{C}`$ transforms the prompt into a structured
scenario specification

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
S=\mathcal{C}(p)=\big(a,\,E,\,Q,\,\mathcal{V},\,u_{\mathrm{ego}},\,C,\,F\big),
``` |  | (1) |

where $`a`$ denotes the V2X safety application under test; $`E`$
describes environmental conditions; $`Q`$ specifies geometric and
traffic-control requirements; $`\mathcal{V}`$ is the roster of
surrounding agents; $`u_{\mathrm{ego}}`$ defines the ego maneuver and
initial conditions; $`C`$ describes the nominal communication
configuration; and $`F=\{F_{1},\ldots,F_{m}\}`$ denotes the set of
communication faults.

Each non-ego vehicle $`i\in\mathcal{V}`$ is characterized by its vehicle
class, semantic role in the interaction, initial distance and speed, V2X
equipage status, and behavioral character. The communication
configuration includes message broadcast rates, communication
parameters, V2X penetration, and the signal plan $`\Psi`$. Each fault
specifies a message-level operator, its target information item, an
event-anchored activation window, and its associated magnitude or
parameters.

#### Physical and Perceived States

Each scenario exercises one V2X application $`a`$, represented as a
decision function

|     |                                |     |     |
|-----|--------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \pi_{a}(\beta,x)\rightarrow u,
       ```                             |     | (2) |

where $`x`$ is the ego physical state, $`\beta`$ is the information
state reconstructed from received V2X messages, and $`u`$ is the
resulting control action. Importantly, the application does not act
directly on the simulator’s ground-truth world state. Its behavior
depends on what information has been sampled, communicated, possibly
degraded, and reconstructed at the receiver.

We represent this transformation through the information chain

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
W\;\xrightarrow{\;\Sigma\;}\;\mathcal{M}\;\xrightarrow{\;\Gamma\;}\;\mathcal{M}^{\prime}\;\xrightarrow{\;\Phi_{F}\;}\;\mathcal{M}^{\prime\prime}\;\xrightarrow{\;\mathcal{B}\;}\;\beta,
``` |  | (3) |

where $`W(t)`$ is the ground-truth world state, $`\Sigma`$ is message
sampling, $`\Gamma`$ is communication-channel delivery, $`\Phi_{F}`$ is
fault injection, and $`\mathcal{B}`$ is receiver-side state
reconstruction. Thus, $`\beta(t)`$ is generally only an imperfect
representation of $`W(t)`$.

A generated message is represented by

|     |                                  |     |     |
|-----|----------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       m_{k}=(t_{k},\hat{t}_{k},y_{k}),
       ```                               |     | (4) |

where $`t_{k}`$ is its true generation time, $`\hat{t}_{k}`$ is the
timestamp reported by the message, and $`y_{k}`$ is its semantic
payload. For information item $`i`$, the receiver retains the most
recent accepted payload,

|     |                              |     |     |
|-----|------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \beta_{i}(t)=y_{k^{\ast},i},
       ```                           |     | (5) |

whose Age of Information is

|     |                                     |     |     |
|-----|-------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \Delta_{i}(t)=t-\hat{t}_{k^{\ast}}.
       ```                                  |     | (6) |

This representation distinguishes three information-failure mechanisms
used throughout the paper. In a *stale-but-detectable* condition, loss
or delay increases $`\Delta_{i}(t)`$ and can trigger a freshness-based
fallback. In a *fresh-but-wrong* condition, messages remain apparently
current while their semantic content differs from the physical world. A
*silent-by-absence* condition occurs when safety-relevant information is
never generated, for example because a conflicting vehicle is not
V2X-equipped.

#### Causal Failure Objective

A difference between $`\beta(t)`$ and $`W(t)`$ is not itself a safety
failure, and an observed collision is not necessarily caused by
communication. The objective of LAST-V2X is therefore to discover
scenarios in which degraded V2X information changes the safety outcome.

For an executed scenario $`S`$, let $`V_{\mathrm{msg}}(S)\in\{0,1\}`$
indicate whether the message-driven ego violates the
application-specific safety criterion, and let
$`V_{\mathrm{gt}}(S)\in\{0,1\}`$ denote the corresponding outcome when
the same application acts on ground-truth information. We define the
causal-admission indicator

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
A(S)=\mathbb{I}\left[V_{\mathrm{msg}}(S)=1\;\wedge\;V_{\mathrm{gt}}(S)=0\right].
``` |  | (7) |

A scenario is therefore admitted as a communication-induced failure only
when the message-driven ego fails while its matched ground-truth control
remains safe.

The primary falsification objective is

|     |                             |     |     |
|-----|-----------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \max_{S\in\mathcal{F}}A(S),
       ```                          |     | (8) |

where $`\mathcal{F}`$ denotes the set of executable specifications
satisfying the schema, analytic feasibility conditions, roadway
constraints, and applicable intent-preservation requirements.

Since $`A(S)`$ is binary and failures can be sparse, the search is
guided before admission by a continuous failure margin $`m(S)`$,

|     |                                                                 |     |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \min_{S^{\prime}\in\mathcal{N}(S)\cap\mathcal{F}}m(S^{\prime}),
       ```                                                              |     | (9) |

where $`\mathcal{N}(S)`$ denotes bounded variations of the current
scenario. Smaller margins indicate scenarios closer to violating the
target safety criterion and are therefore prioritized during refinement.
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Failure Margin and Search Settings ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications")
defines $`m(S)`$ and the search settings.

Once an admitted failure has been identified, the objective changes from
discovery to explanation. Let $`F(S)`$ denote its injected fault set.
The minimal-witness problem is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
F^{\ast}=\mathop{\arg\min}_{F^{\prime}\subseteq F(S)}|F^{\prime}|\qquad\mathrm{s.t.}\qquad A(S[F^{\prime}])=1,
``` |  | (10) |

so the final artifact retains only the smallest fault configuration
required to reproduce the communication-caused failure; for a
silent-by-absence failure, $`F(S)=\emptyset`$ and the witness is the
unfaulted scenario itself. At the benchmark level, multiple such
witnesses are sought across different applications, fault classes,
penetration levels, and conflict geometries rather than repeatedly
maximizing the severity of a single mechanism.

The four modules below implement this process from language
interpretation to causally verified failure discovery.

### 2.2 Module I: LLM Agent Analysis

The first module converts an open-ended natural-language request into a
structured V2X test that is both syntactically valid and analytically
capable of exercising the intended communication mechanism. It combines
a schema-constrained LLM semantic parser with a deterministic
feasibility verifier. The LLM determines what the prompt means; explicit
rules and arithmetic determine whether that interpretation can produce a
meaningful test.

#### Schema-Constrained Intent Parsing

Let $`\Lambda`$ denote the language interpretation operator. Given
prompt $`p`$, it produces an initial candidate specification

|     |                     |     |      |
|-----|---------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       S^{(0)}=\Lambda(p).
       ```                  |     | (11) |

The parser uses structured JSON output constrained by the schema of
Eq. ([1](#S2.E1 "In Scenario Specification ‣ 2.1 Problem Description ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications")).
It identifies the application under test, environment and map
requirements, ego and surrounding-agent attributes, communication
configuration, and requested faults. When the prompt does not explicitly
name the safety application, $`\Lambda`$ infers it from the traffic
interaction. Explicitly specified communication conditions are
preserved, whereas unspecified fields are filled from predefined nominal
defaults rather than through unconstrained generation.

Parsing is implemented as a bounded repair loop. If a candidate
specification violates the schema or fails the analytic verifier, its
diagnostic feedback is returned to the same interpretation operator:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
S^{(k+1)}=\Lambda\left(p,\,S^{(k)},\,\mathcal{E}(S^{(k)})\right),
``` |  | (12) |

where $`\mathcal{E}(S^{(k)})`$ contains machine-readable violations
together with actionable repair guidance. The LLM therefore performs
semantic interpretation and repair, while the admissible specification
space remains controlled by explicit constraints.
Appendix [F](#A6 "Appendix F LLM Prompts ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications")
gives the parser, planner, and reflection prompts in condensed form.

#### Analytic Feasibility Verification

The verifier determines whether a candidate can realize the
communication condition it claims to test before simulator resources are
committed. For a temporal fault $`F_{j}`$, realizability is evaluated
against the freshness budget $`B_{a}`$ of the information stream
consumed by application $`a`$. A fault is potentially consequential when

|     |                                 |     |      |
|-----|---------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \overline{\Delta}(F_{j})>B_{a},
       ```                              |     | (13) |

where $`\overline{\Delta}(F_{j})`$ is a lower bound on the peak Age of
Information (AoI) \[[60](#bib.bib44)\] induced by the fault. For a
stream with broadcast period $`T_{s}`$ and nominal latency $`L`$,
dropping $`k`$ consecutive messages gives

|     |                             |     |      |
|-----|-----------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \overline{\Delta}=kT_{s}+L,
       ```                          |     | (14) |

whereas an additional communication delay $`d`$ gives

|     |                        |     |      |
|-----|------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \overline{\Delta}=L+d.
       ```                     |     | (15) |

The true peak can exceed these bounds by up to one broadcast period,
since that much time may already have passed since the last delivery; a
fault that satisfies $`\overline{\Delta}(F_{j})>B_{a}`$ is therefore
guaranteed to breach the budget. If a requested drop is too weak, for
example, the verifier can return the smallest count whose bound reaches
the budget

|     |                                                        |     |      |
|-----|--------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       k^{\ast}=\left\lceil\frac{B_{a}-L}{T_{s}}\right\rceil.
       ```                                                     |     | (16) |

Semantic-content faults require a different test because they can remain
apparently fresh. For a frozen SPaT value, incorrect MAP binding, or
perturbed BSM position, the verifier checks whether the targeted
information item is actually consumed by application $`a`$, whether the
activation window overlaps a relevant decision period, and whether the
requested corruption can produce $`\beta(t)\neq W(t)`$.

Additional checks cover fault-window validity, conflict timing, V2X
equipage consistency, nominal communication settings, and roadway
satisfiability. Blocking violations are returned through $`\mathcal{E}`$
to the parser. The same verification gate is later reused to eliminate
infeasible mutants during Scenario Refinement.
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Verifier Check Families ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications")
lists all check families.

### 2.3 Module II: Retrieval-Augmented Scenario Grounding

A verified specification describes what interaction should occur, but it
is still symbolic. It does not yet identify where that interaction can
physically occur, which concrete lanes correspond to semantic roles such
as “crossing from the left,” or how the specified agents should behave.
The second module therefore binds the specification to retrieved
roadway, V2X, and behavioral knowledge \[[61](#bib.bib50)\] and produces
a replayable scenario program.

#### Signal-Semantic Road Retrieval

A signal-semantic road graph $`\mathcal{G}`$ is constructed offline from
the OpenDRIVE map of each simulator town. Unlike a conventional road
graph that records only coarse topology or whether an intersection is
signalized, $`\mathcal{G}`$ preserves controller identity,
traffic-signal identity, junction connections, controlled movements, and
signal groups. These quantities are required not only for geometric
grounding but also because SPaT and MAP faults directly operate on them.

The basic retrieval unit is

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\ell=(\mathrm{junction},\mathrm{movement},\mathrm{signal\ group},\mathbf{f}_{\ell}),
``` |  |

where $`\mathbf{f}_{\ell}`$ records geometric and traffic-control
attributes. Given application $`a`$ and map query $`Q`$, the candidate
set is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}(S)=\left\{\ell\in\mathcal{G}:\mathrm{pre}(a)(\mathbf{f}_{\ell})\wedge q_{Q}(\ell)\right\},
``` |  | (17) |

where $`\mathrm{pre}(a)`$ encodes the geometric preconditions of the
target application and $`q_{Q}`$ applies the map requirements inferred
from the prompt. A seeded deterministic rule selects $`\ell^{\ast}`$
from the feasible set. If no candidate exists, the failed constraint is
returned to Module I for repair.

#### V2X and Driver-Behavior Retrieval

A second knowledge base contains the V2X semantics required to convert
the traffic scene into a safety test. It represents the three message
streams implemented by LAST-V2X: SPaT messages describing signal phase
and timing, MAP messages describing intersection geometry and
lane-to-signal-group associations, and BSMs describing the states of
equipped vehicles.

An application registry maps each application $`a`$ to the information
streams it consumes, its geometric preconditions, and its
information-quality budgets. A fault-pattern library maps
natural-language communication degradations to the protocol-level fault
operators implemented by the runtime.

Driver behavior is instantiated through parameterized templates. For
vehicle $`i`$,

|     |                                                      |     |      |
|-----|------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \theta_{i}=w_{E}\odot T_{\mathrm{beh}}(c_{i},b_{i}),
       ```                                                   |     | (18) |

where $`T_{\mathrm{beh}}`$ maps vehicle class $`c_{i}`$ and behavioral
character $`b_{i}`$ to parameters including desired speed, time headway,
standstill clearance, reaction time, comfortable deceleration, and
signal compliance. Environmental weighting $`w_{E}`$ adjusts these
parameters according to $`E`$.

#### Lane-Level Scene Planning

The retrieved movement unit determines a feasible junction, but each
semantic agent role must still be mapped onto an actual lane. The
executor queries the selected junction in the live simulator and
constructs an admissible approach set $`\mathcal{J}(\ell^{\ast})`$
containing lane identifiers, movement directions, and measured headings
relative to the ego approach.

A constrained planning operator assigns agents to these retrieved
approaches:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{Z}=\Lambda_{\mathrm{plan}}\left(S,\mathcal{J}(\ell^{\ast})\right).
``` |  | (19) |

The LLM may therefore resolve semantic relationships such as “oncoming”
or “crossing from the left,” but it cannot invent lanes or roadway
geometry.

Each assignment is then validated deterministically. Using the specified
spawn distance and initial speed, the validator checks whether the
relevant vehicles can reach the conflict region within the required
encounter window. Invalid assignments are rejected and deterministic
grounding heuristics are used as a fallback where necessary.

#### Scenario Program Assembly

Finally, the verified specification, retrieved movement, lane
assignments $`\mathcal{Z}`$, and behavior parameters are combined
through

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
P=\mathrm{bind}\left(S,\ell^{\ast},\mathcal{Z},\{\theta_{i}\}\right).
``` |  | (20) |

The resulting program contains the agent routes, signal plan $`\Psi`$,
V2X message streams, communication settings, event-anchored fault
schedule, and monitoring configuration required for execution.

Importantly, $`P`$ is typed scenario data consumed by a fixed runtime
engine; it is not LLM-generated simulator source code. This makes each
test reproducible, allows later refinement operators to manipulate the
specification symbolically, and preserves traceability between the
executable scenario and the original prompt or retrieved knowledge.

### 2.4 Module III: Automated V2X Scenario Synthesis

The third module executes the grounded scenario program as a coupled
physical–information process. Unlike a conventional traffic simulation
that models vehicle motion alone, LAST-V2X synchronously advances the
traffic state, signal state, V2X messages, receiver-side estimated
state, application decisions, and paired ego outcomes. Execution
produces the synchronized trace

|     |                               |     |      |
|-----|-------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \mathcal{T}=\mathrm{Exec}(P).
       ```                            |     | (21) |

#### Synchronous Physical–Information Execution

Simulation proceeds synchronously with fixed step $`\Delta t=50`$ ms. At
each tick, messages are sampled from the current world, propagated
through the communication channel, degraded by any active faults, and
incorporated into the estimated information state. The application then
acts on that estimate:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\beta_{t+\Delta t}=\mathcal{B}\left(\beta_{t},\,(\Phi_{F}\circ\Gamma\circ\Sigma)(W_{t})\right),
``` |  | (22) |

followed by

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
W_{t+\Delta t}=\Phi_{\mathrm{sim}}\left(W_{t},\,\pi_{a}(\beta_{t},x_{t}^{\mathrm{msg}}),\,u_{t},\,\Psi_{t}\right),
``` |  | (23) |

where $`u_{t}`$ contains the controls of the non-ego agents.

Vehicle routes are instantiated on the live simulator map, initial
conditions are stabilized before the critical encounter,
conflict-relevant agents follow the scripted controllers parameterized
by $`\theta_{i}`$, and background traffic is controlled through a seeded
Traffic Manager. The signal plan is aligned with the intended encounter
so that event-anchored communication faults occur relative to the
corresponding traffic or signal event rather than at an arbitrary
simulation time.

#### Spatial V2X Communication Channel

The communication operator $`\Gamma`$ models delivery as a function of
the instantaneous physical relationship between transmitter and
receiver. For each link, latency $`L`$ and delivery probability
$`p_{\mathrm{del}}`$ are obtained from received signal strength:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
(L,p_{\mathrm{del}})=g(\mathrm{RSSI}),\qquad\mathrm{RSSI}=P_{\mathrm{tx}}-10n\log_{10}d-B_{\mathrm{blk}}(x_{\mathrm{tx}},x_{\mathrm{rx}}),
``` |  | (24) |

where $`P_{\mathrm{tx}}`$ is transmit power, $`n`$ is the path-loss
exponent, $`d`$ is transmitter–receiver distance, and
$`B_{\mathrm{blk}}`$ is the height-aware building-blockage term. The
mapping $`g`$ increases latency and reduces delivery probability as
signal strength deteriorates.

Roadside units are placed at physical signal-pole locations, so
communication quality evolves with vehicle motion, urban geometry, and
transmitter placement rather than being represented by one scenario-wide
packet-loss rate.
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Channel Model Details ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications")
gives the complete model and its default parameters.

#### Semantic V2X Fault Injection

After nominal channel propagation, the fault engine $`\Phi_{F}`$ applies
protocol-level message faults. Seven operators are implemented across
three failure families. Delivery faults include drop, burst_drop, and
delay; the timestamp fault skew changes the reported generation time;
and semantic-content faults include freeze, rebind, and pos_perturb.
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Fault Operators ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications")
defines each operator and its parameters.

These operators alter different parts of the information chain. Delivery
and timing faults primarily change message availability or apparent age,
whereas semantic faults may preserve normal delivery and fresh
timestamps while changing the represented state. Fault windows are
anchored to traffic or signal events and converted into deterministic
simulation-time intervals, allowing identical tests to be reproduced
across paired executions and subsequent replays.

#### Paired Counterfactual Execution

A shadow ground-truth ego is propagated alongside the message-driven
ego. Both use the same application, controller, route, initial
condition, traffic scene, and simulation seed. Their only systematic
difference is the information provided to the application: the
message-driven ego acts on $`\beta(t)`$, whereas the ground-truth ego
acts on the corresponding state derived directly from $`W(t)`$.

The shadow ego has no physical presence and therefore cannot alter
surrounding traffic. This paired construction provides the
counterfactual required by
Eq. ([7](#S2.E7 "In Causal Failure Objective ‣ 2.1 Problem Description ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications")).
Each simulation tick records physical state, signal state, message
transmissions and receptions, reconstructed information, application
decisions, and both ego outcomes. The resulting trace $`\mathcal{T}`$
therefore provides an auditable record of the complete chain from
communication degradation to behavioral consequence.

### 2.5 Module IV: Scenario Refinement

1: prompt $`p^{(0)}`$, goal $`g`$, budgets $`N_{r}`$, $`N_{s}`$, elite
size $`K`$

2: minimal witnesses, or diagnoses $`\{\mathcal{D}^{(r)}\}`$

3: for $`r=0,\dots,N_{r}-1`$ do $`\triangleright`$ reflection

4:   $`S\leftarrow\mathcal{C}(p^{(r)})`$; 
$`\mathcal{T}\leftarrow\mathrm{Exec}(P)`$ $`\triangleright`$ Mod. I–III

5:   if $`A(S)=1`$ then return $`\textsc{DeltaDebug}(S)`$

6:   $`\mathcal{S}\leftarrow\{S\}`$;  $`\mathcal{H}\leftarrow\emptyset`$
$`\triangleright`$ elite, admitted

7:   for $`b=1,\dots,N_{s}`$ do $`\triangleright`$ search

8:
   $`S^{\prime}\leftarrow\textsc{Mutate}\big(\textsc{Sample}_{w}(\mathcal{S})\big)`$

9:    if $`\neg\textsc{Verify}(S^{\prime})`$ then continue
$`\triangleright`$ gated

10:    execute $`S^{\prime}`$; compute $`m(S^{\prime})`$

11:    if $`A(S^{\prime})=1`$ then
$`\mathcal{H}\leftarrow\mathcal{H}\cup\{S^{\prime}\}`$
$`\triangleright`$ catalog

12:
   $`\mathcal{S}\leftarrow\textsc{Top}_{K}(\mathcal{S}\cup\{S^{\prime}\})`$
by $`w`$

13:   end for

14:   if $`\mathcal{H}\neq\emptyset`$ then return
$`\textsc{DeltaDebug}(\mathcal{H})`$

15:   $`\mathcal{D}^{(r)}\leftarrow\textsc{Digest}(\mathcal{T},\ldots)`$

16:
  $`p^{(r+1)}\leftarrow\Lambda_{\mathrm{ref}}(p^{(r)},\mathcal{D}^{(r)},g)`$
$`\triangleright`$ Eq. ([27](#S2.E27 "In Prompt-Space Reflection ‣ 2.5 Module IV: Scenario Refinement ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications"))

17: end for

18: return $`\{\mathcal{D}^{(r)}\}_{r=0}^{N_{r}-1}`$
$`\triangleright`$ no admission

Algorithm 1 Scenario refinement by search and reflection.

A single execution may expose an admitted failure, but many initial
tests are too weak, mistimed, or otherwise poorly configured to make the
intended communication mechanism consequential. Scenario Refinement
therefore closes the loop between simulation evidence and scenario
generation.

Two complementary refinement processes are used. An inner
*specification-space search* varies bounded properties of the current
grounded scenario while preserving its semantic intent. An outer
*prompt-space reflection* revises the natural-language test description
when the execution evidence indicates that the original intent itself
prevents the desired mechanism from becoming consequential.
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 2.5 Module IV: Scenario Refinement ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications")
summarizes both loops.

#### Execution Diagnosis and Causal Admission

The refinement monitor first identifies intervals in which a
safety-relevant estimated information item differs from its
corresponding ground-truth state,

|     |                            |     |      |
|-----|----------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \beta_{i}(t)\neq W_{i}(t).
       ```                         |     | (25) |

Each divergence episode is related to the next application decision
through a *hazard slack* $`\delta`$. Negative slack indicates that a
decision was made while the estimated state was incorrect, whereas a
small positive value denotes a near miss. Expected absences, such as
missing BSMs from unequipped vehicles, are labeled separately as
structural silent-by-absence conditions.

The paired rollout then evaluates the admission criterion of
Eq. ([7](#S2.E7 "In Causal Failure Objective ‣ 2.1 Problem Description ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications")).
If both egos violate the safety criterion, the scenario is treated as
non-attributable because the underlying traffic interaction itself is
unsafe. If neither fails, the trace remains useful for determining how
close the communication-induced divergence came to changing the outcome.
Only

|     |                                             |     |
|-----|---------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       V_{\mathrm{msg}}=1,\qquad V_{\mathrm{gt}}=0
       ```                                          |     |

constitutes a communication-caused failure.

#### Specification-Space Search

When the current specification is valid but does not produce an admitted
failure, the inner loop searches a bounded neighborhood of that
scenario. Candidate mutations modify parameters including fault type,
magnitude and activation window, vehicle distance and speed, and V2X
penetration. These changes preserve the high-level test intent while
altering how strongly the information degradation overlaps the
safety-critical interaction.

Every proposed mutant is first passed through the analytic verifier.
Feasible mutants are executed and ranked using failure margin $`m(S)`$.
Candidates closer to failure receive greater probability of producing
descendants according to

|     |                          |     |      |
|-----|--------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       w(S)=\frac{1}{1/2+m(S)}.
       ```                       |     | (26) |

Thus, execution-derived near misses focus subsequent search without
replacing the causal admission test itself.

Search is also coverage-oriented. Admitted scenarios are cataloged by
mechanism dimensions including application, fault family, V2X
penetration, and conflict geometry, discouraging repeated discovery of
equivalent failures.

Each admitted scenario is then minimized by delta debugging, a greedy
descent: at every step it tries each single weakening of the fault
vector (removing a fault, halving its magnitude, or shortening its
window) and keeps the first that preserves admission under the same
paired causal test, stopping when none does. The result approximates the
minimal-witness objective of
Eq. ([10](#S2.E10 "In Causal Failure Objective ‣ 2.1 Problem Description ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications")):
it is 1-minimal, in that no single fault can be removed or weakened
without losing the failure, and it yields a replayable scenario
containing only the communication degradation necessary for the failure.

#### Prompt-Space Reflection

Bounded specification mutation cannot repair every unsuccessful test. In
some cases, the natural-language intent itself makes the requested
failure mechanism irrelevant. For example, a prompt may activate a SPaT
freeze only after the ego has already completed the safety-critical
decision. Increasing the magnitude of that fault cannot make it causal
without changing its temporal relationship to the described event.

The outer loop therefore constructs an evidence digest
$`\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{T}^{(r)})`$ containing the paired outcomes,
divergence episodes, hazard slack, decision-epoch AoI, failure margins,
and verifier diagnostics. Following verbal self-reflection and
self-refinement for LLM agents \[[62](#bib.bib45), [63](#bib.bib46)\], a
dedicated reflection operator then updates the prompt:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
p^{(r+1)}=\Lambda_{\mathrm{ref}}\left(p^{(r)},\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{T}^{(r)}),g\right).
``` |  | (27) |

The purpose of reflection is to diagnose why the intended mechanism
failed to affect the application and revise the test description
accordingly. It may, for example, move a fault window so that it
overlaps the decision, extend a semantic corruption through a signal
transition, or modify a described geometry that prevents communication
exposure.

The reflected prompt receives no privileged execution path. It re-enters
Module I and is parsed and analytically verified, is grounded again
through Module II, and is executed through Module III under the same
causal admission criterion. Reflection therefore cannot directly
manipulate simulator state or force a violation; it can only propose a
revised test whose validity and causal effect must again be established
by the complete pipeline.

## 3 Experimental Results

The experiments evaluate the three main capabilities of LAST-V2X:
language-driven V2X scenario generation, causal verification of
communication-induced failures, and adaptive refinement of ineffective
tests. A 100-scene benchmark first evaluates whether natural-language
scenarios can be generated reliably without producing false failures.
Communication-fault experiments then test whether the paired execution
can distinguish communication-induced failures from unsafe traffic
interactions. Finally, a 50-scene refinement study evaluates whether
parameter search and LLM self-reflection can systematically turn
ineffective tests into causally verified failures. Ablation studies
isolate the contribution of the key components.

### 3.1 Experiment Setup

#### Implementation and Protocol

All experiments use the complete LAST-V2X pipeline with synchronous
CARLA simulation across eight towns, except the specification-space
search runs of the refinement study, which use a lightweight stub
backend. GPT-4o \[[64](#bib.bib27)\] is used for language parsing,
planning, and reflection with temperature 0.2 and a fixed sampling seed.
Scenario seeds control vehicle equipage, communication loss, RSU
selection, vehicle blueprints, and retrieval tie-breaking, enabling
deterministic replay. For each scene, LAST-V2X records the generated
specification, grounding results, execution traces, safety outcomes, and
communication states. The evaluation includes 112 live CARLA scenes; 110
prompts compile on the first attempt and two require verifier-guided
correction. Unless otherwise stated, results are reported from
deterministic single-seed runs.
Appendix [G](#A7 "Appendix G Reproducibility ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications")
summarizes the configuration of each experiment.

#### Safety Applications

We evaluate six V2X safety applications, summarized in
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Safety Applications ‣ 3.1 Experiment Setup ‣ 3 Experimental Results ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications").
RLVW and GLOSA are *signal applications* that primarily use
infrastructure-to-vehicle information, while IMA, LTA, FCW, and EEBL are
*conflict applications* that primarily use vehicle-to-vehicle BSMs. This
distinction captures two important V2X settings: infrastructure
information can be shared by multiple vehicles, whereas a missing BSM
can make a conflicting vehicle invisible to the receiving application.
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Safety Application Logic ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications")
gives each application’s decision rule and violation criterion.

|  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|
|  |  |  | Age budget (s) |  | Position |
| Application | Full name |  Function | SPaT | BSM | error (m) |
| Signal applications infrastructure-to-vehicle (SPaT/MAP) |  |  |  |  |  |
| RLVW | Red-Light Violation Warning |  Warns against entering on red | 1.0 | – | – |
| GLOSA | Green Light Optimal Speed Advisory |  Recommends speed for a green arrival | 1.0 | – | – |
| Conflict applications vehicle-to-vehicle (BSM) |  |  |  |  |  |
| IMA | Intersection Movement Assist |  Warns of crossing-vehicle conflicts | – | 0.5 | 1.5 |
| LTA | Left Turn Assist |  Warns of conflicting opposing traffic | 1.0 | 0.5 | 1.5 |
| FCW | Forward Collision Warning |  Warns of a slower or stopped lead vehicle | – | 0.3 | 1.5 |
| EEBL | Emergency Electronic Brake Light |  Relays a hard-braking event ahead | – | 0.3 | – |

Table 1: V2X safety applications and their message requirements (SAE
J2945/1 \[[65](#bib.bib47)\]). Age budgets bound the staleness of the
consumed SPaT or BSM stream; “–” marks a quantity the application does
not use.

#### Experiment Groups

![Refer to caption](2610.30979v1/fig_track_generation_v20.png)

Figure 2: 100 generated scenes. a, Application and town. b, Driving
quality (RF, route following; ACC, acceleration; YV, yaw rate; LI, lane
invasion; CE, communication exposure). c, Scene conditions. d, Minimum
gap. e, Examples.

The evaluation contains three main experiment groups. First, a 100-scene
normal-traffic benchmark tests whether natural-language descriptions can
be converted into valid V2X scenarios without producing false
communication-induced failures. The prompts describe only the traffic
scene and environment; the exercised application, town, and nominal
communication configuration are inferred or assigned by the pipeline.
The benchmark spans all six applications and all eight CARLA towns,
together with varied weather, times of day, and vehicle classes
(Fig. [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Experiment Groups ‣ 3.1 Experiment Setup ‣ 3 Experimental Results ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications")a,c).
Second, a communication-fault suite evaluates whether LAST-V2X can
distinguish failures caused by degraded V2X information from those
caused by the underlying traffic interaction. Third, the suite is
extended to 50 scenarios to evaluate adaptive refinement through
specification-space search and LLM self-reflection. Corridor, multi-CV,
and channel-sensitivity experiments are treated as supplementary
studies.

#### Evaluation Metrics

Metrics are organized at four levels. The *run level* determines whether
communication caused a safety failure. Each executed scenario is
classified as Admitted, Non-attributable, or Clean. Admitted means the
degraded-information rollout violates the safety criterion while the
matched non-degraded rollout does not. Non-attributable means both
rollouts violate, indicating that the failure cannot be attributed to
communication. Clean means neither rollout violates. Scenarios rejected
before execution are labeled Gated.

For scenarios with a measurable conflict gap, we also report

|     |                                         |     |      |
|-----|-----------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \Delta g=g^{\mathrm{t}}-g^{\mathrm{b}},
       ```                                      |     | (28) |

where $`g^{\mathrm{t}}`$ and $`g^{\mathrm{b}}`$ are the minimum conflict
gaps under non-degraded and degraded V2X information, respectively.
Positive $`\Delta g`$ indicates a loss of physical separation caused by
degraded information.

The *estimated-state level* measures how strongly the vehicle’s
perceived state deviates from the physical state. We report hazard
slack, decision-epoch Age of Information (AoI), and the type and
duration of each estimate–truth divergence. The *search level* measures
refinement efficiency. We report the number of admitted failures,
attribution rate, feasibility-gate rejection rate, executions required
to reach the first admission, and minimal-witness size after delta
debugging. The *realization level* verifies that the generated scene was
executed as intended. Parse success, spawn audits, and route completion
are used to detect realization artifacts, while the 100-scene
normal-traffic benchmark serves as a negative control for false
admissions.

### 3.2 Scenario Generation at Scale

![Refer to caption](2610.30979v1/fig_scene_d13_flatA_v4_style4.png)

Figure 3: A nine-agent left turn in Town03 under a healthy channel. a,
Prompt and compiled specification. b, Six instants from four viewpoints.
c, Agent paths and V2I range. d, True and estimated signal phases. e,
Message deliveries.

The first experiment evaluates whether plain traffic language can drive
the full pipeline at scale.
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Experiment Groups ‣ 3.1 Experiment Setup ‣ 3 Experimental Results ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications")
summarizes the 100-scene normal-traffic benchmark. The prompts describe
only the traffic scene and environment: they do not name the exercised
V2X application, the CARLA town, or any communication fault. The
application is inferred by the parser, feasible towns are identified
through retrieval, and the benchmark harness assigns the least-used
feasible town. As a result, coverage is measured rather than
hand-designed. The benchmark covers six V2X applications across eight
CARLA towns, with various weather conditions, times of day, vehicle
classes, and traffic densities ranging from a single ego vehicle to
eleven agents.

Generation is both reliable and faithful. All 100 scenes compile into
valid and feasible specifications within at most two parse attempts,
with an average of 1.58 attempts per scene, and every scene is grounded
to a feasible movement unit and executed to completion. The only
recurring compile issue is an out-of-vocabulary maneuver field, which is
corrected on retry. Realization quality is also high: 365 of 367 vehicle
spawns are clean, all 2048 checked lane markings match the authored
OpenDRIVE map, and 253 of 254 vehicles remain on route.

Most importantly, the normal-traffic corpus yields zero admitted
communication-induced failures under healthy communication, confirming
that LAST-V2X does not manufacture failures. The generated scenes also
remain physically well behaved, with zero collisions, zero out-of-road
distance, and sub-0.15 m tracking error in both rollouts. The paired
executions further provide a scene-level measure of information impact.
Among the 79 scenes with finite conflict gaps in both rollouts, the
ground-truth ego maintains more than 0.5 m additional separation in 33
scenes, with a median gain of 8.5 m and a maximum of 112.3 m.
Figure [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3.2 Scenario Generation at Scale ‣ 3 Experimental Results ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications")
shows one representative dense control scene in detail. Overall, these
results show that plain traffic language is sufficient to drive LAST-V2X
to broad and faithful V2X scenario generation without introducing
spurious failures.

### 3.3 Corridor Traversal along an RSU Chain

![Refer to caption](2610.30979v1/fig_track_corridor_prompt_v18.png)

Figure 4: Corridor traversal along an RSU chain. a, Shared prompt; $`C`$
is the condition-specific clause. b, Clause, parsed value, and 10-seed
results per condition, relative to No V2X. c, Camera frames on the
retrieved corridor. d, Junctions with known SPaT. e,f, Ego speed without
and with traffic.

The corridor study measures what infrastructure ahead of the trip buys:
a connected vehicle’s information horizon need not end at its own radio.
Like the main benchmark, it is driven from language
(Fig. [4](#S3.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 3.3 Corridor Traversal along an RSU Chain ‣ 3 Experimental Results ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications")a).
One prompt describes the corridor, four signalized junctions with a
shared 6/3/12 s plan and offsets timed against a free-flowing driver,
and differs between runs only in whether the road is empty or the ego
follows eight unequipped cars, and in one information clause
(Fig. [4](#S3.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 3.3 Corridor Traversal along an RSU Chain ‣ 3 Experimental Results ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications")b):
no V2X; *direct* SPaT, where each junction’s RSU broadcasts only its own
timing over a 50 m radio; and an *RSU relay chain*, where
backhaul-connected RSUs rebroadcast the whole corridor’s SPaT at 5 ms
per hop, so one reachable RSU delivers every junction ahead. All six
prompts compile to the intended condition on the first parse; the
verifier’s only repairs lengthen a too-short episode. Retrieval binds
the corridor to a Town05 arterial with junctions 91, 88 and 54 m apart,
and the harness then sweeps the offset plan (aligned, green wave,
adverse), the radio range (50, 100, 150 m) and 10 seeds: 420 CARLA runs
with no red-light entry and no collision.

The chain’s value concentrates where the radio is weakest. At
$`R=50`$ m, below the junction spacing, direct coverage is intermittent,
and the relay lifts the mean number of junctions known ahead from 0.5 to
2.6
(Fig. [4](#S3.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 3.3 Corridor Traversal along an RSU Chain ‣ 3 Experimental Results ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications")d).
With the horizon comes smoothness. Against adverse offsets on the empty
corridor, GLOSA over the chained SPaT cuts stops from 1.9 to 1.0 and the
mean acceleration magnitude from 1.70 to 1.21 m/s² relative to no V2X,
while direct SPaT at the same range changes little (1.9 stops,
1.62 m/s²;
Fig. [4](#S3.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 3.3 Corridor Traversal along an RSU Chain ‣ 3 Experimental Results ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications")b);
between J1 and J3 the relayed ego holds about 10 m/s where the others
brake and re-accelerate
(Fig. [4](#S3.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 3.3 Corridor Traversal along an RSU Chain ‣ 3 Experimental Results ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications")e).
Travel time stays signal-bound (47.4 s without V2X versus 46.6 s with
the relay chain), and the one stop that remains, at the first light,
which every condition meets on red, is slightly longer than the no-V2X
ego’s total stopped time (11.6 versus 10.5 s): the corridor’s benefit is
fewer stops and gentler control, not higher speed. The chain at
$`R=50`$ m matches direct SPaT at three times the range (1.0 stops,
1.23 m/s² at 150 m); infrastructure cooperation substitutes for radio
range.

With the eight-car platoon ahead, the queue sets the pace and travel
time is the same in all three conditions (98 s, averaged over the offset
plans). What changes is how that time is spent: the relay chain cuts the
ego’s time stopped from 31.2 to 21.5 s and its mean acceleration
magnitude from 0.88 to 0.74 m/s², while direct SPaT, whose short radio
rarely sees past the queue, changes neither (31.3 s, 0.86 m/s²;
Fig. [4](#S3.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 3.3 Corridor Traversal along an RSU Chain ‣ 3 Experimental Results ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications")b,f).
The effect is largest under the green-wave plan, where idling falls from
34.0 to 13.3 s: the ego glides toward queues it knows will discharge
instead of braking into them. In traffic, corridor information buys
smoothness rather than time.

### 3.4 Cooperative Scenarios with Multiple Connected Vehicles

![Refer to caption](2610.30979v1/fig_track_multicv_prompt_v10.png)

Figure 5: Multi-CV cooperation: EEBL relay chain (a–d) and IMA mutual
yield (e–h). a,e, Prompts. b,f, Retrieved scenes. c, CV3 speed and gap.
g, Distance between the crossing vehicles. d,h, Clause, CARLA frame, and
10-seed results per condition.

The multi-CV study makes cooperation itself the object under test: with
every connected vehicle owning an estimated-state store and a decision
policy, what two vehicles achieve together becomes measurable
(Fig. [5](#S3.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 3.4 Cooperative Scenarios with Multiple Connected Vehicles ‣ 3 Experimental Results ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications")).
Both experiments are again stated in language, one prompt per condition,
and all six prompts compile to the intended condition on the first
parse; retrieval binds the brake-warning chain to a straight Town05
arterial and the crossing to Town05 junction 1722, and each condition
runs for 10 seeds. In the EEBL V2V relay chain, a lead vehicle brakes
hard beyond the third vehicle’s radio range and behind an occluding
second vehicle, so whether CV3 learns of the event in time depends on
whether CV2 rebroadcasts the warning vehicle-to-vehicle. With the V2V
relay, CV3 brakes 1.49 s after the lead and keeps a 22.7 m minimum gap,
with no collision in 10 seeds. Without it, CV3 waits 3.52 s for visual
evidence, the gap closes to 0.1 m and 7 of 10 runs end in a rear-end
collision; with CV2 unequipped, CV3 brakes after 4.21 s and 9 of 10 runs
collide
(Fig. [5](#S3.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 3.4 Cooperative Scenarios with Multiple Connected Vehicles ‣ 3 Experimental Results ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications")c,d).
The V2V relay hop converts an occluding vehicle into infrastructure
worth 2.0 s of warning.

The IMA mutual-yield experiment measures the other face of cooperation.
Two crossing vehicles timed to conflict interleave cleanly when both are
equipped: a 12.7 m closest approach and a 2.04 s post-encroachment time,
with the later arrival yielding in 10 of 10 seeds. With one or neither
equipped, the encounter degenerates to a 5.6 m near miss with a 0.28 s
post-encroachment time and contact in 2 of 10 seeds, identically in both
cases
(Fig. [5](#S3.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 3.4 Cooperative Scenarios with Multiple Connected Vehicles ‣ 3 Experimental Results ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications")g,h).
Cooperation is pairwise: one-sided equipage buys nothing when the
counterpart is silent. This restates the corpus’s silent-miss finding at
the scale of two deciding vehicles.

### 3.5 Scenario Refinement at Scale

Figure 6: Scenario refinement on the 50-scene fault suite. a, Outcome by
fault class. b, Executions or prompt revisions to first admission. c,
Median best margin during search (shaded: IQR).

The refinement experiment evaluates whether ineffective V2X tests can be
systematically improved through specification-space search and LLM
self-reflection. The fault suite is expanded from 12 to 50 prompts
spanning six applications and diverse communication faults, including
intentionally weak, mistimed, and ineffective cases. All scenarios are
first executed without refinement. The 43 non-admitted cases are then
refined using specification-space search with a budget of 120 candidate
mutants per scene and LLM self-reflection with up to five revisions. To
measure each mechanism’s contribution, the two loops of
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 2.5 Module IV: Scenario Refinement ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications")
are applied separately to every target: search mutates the compiled
scenario, and reflection revises the prompt, with each revision compiled
and executed once.

The initial execution admits only 7 of the 50 scenarios. Most missing,
delayed, or stale messages do not produce failures because the
application can detect or tolerate them, whereas incorrect but
apparently valid information is more likely to alter vehicle behavior.
This result reinforces an important point: injecting a communication
fault does not by itself create a meaningful V2X safety test.

Across the 50 scenarios, refinement increases admitted failures from 7
to 32
(Fig. [6](#S3.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 3.5 Scenario Refinement at Scale ‣ 3 Experimental Results ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications")a).
Specification-space search finds failures in 23 of the 43 refinement
targets, with a median of 8 executions to the first admission and no
successful case requiring more than 27 executions. LLM self-reflection
rescues 8 targets, typically within one revised prompt
(Fig. [6](#S3.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 3.5 Scenario Refinement at Scale ‣ 3 Experimental Results ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications")b).
Six of these are also reachable through parameter search, while two
require semantic changes beyond the bounded search space. The two
refinement mechanisms are therefore complementary: search adjusts
quantitative conditions such as fault timing and interaction severity,
whereas self-reflection repairs semantically or structurally ineffective
test intents.

For scenarios successfully converted by search, the best safety margin
decreases to a median of 7% of its initial value, compared with 80% for
scenarios that remain fail-safe
(Fig. [6](#S3.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 3.5 Scenario Refinement at Scale ‣ 3 Experimental Results ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications")c).
Delta debugging further reduces each admitted case to a 1-minimal
witness with a single fault. Of the 18 scenarios that remain
non-admitted, most either fail under both communication conditions and
are therefore non-attributable, or remain fail-safe despite refinement.
These results show that LAST-V2X can systematically improve ineffective
tests without forcing every scenario into an unsafe outcome.

Figure [7](#S3.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ 3.5 Scenario Refinement at Scale ‣ 3 Experimental Results ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications")
illustrates how self-reflection repairs an ineffective test. In
rlvw_late_freeze, the original SPaT freeze begins after the ego has
already made its stopping decision, so the scenario remains clean. Using
the execution evidence, the LLM identifies the mistimed fault and
revises the scenario so that the frozen SPaT persists through the
critical decision window. After refinement, the message-driven ego
enters the intersection on red while the matched non-degraded ego stops,
converting the original scenario into a causally verified
communication-induced failure.

![Refer to caption](2610.30979v1/fig_refinement_case_v4.png)

Figure 7: Refinement example rlvw_late_freeze. a, Prompt revisions by
LLM self-reflection. b,c, Paired runs of the original and revised
prompts: ego and ground-truth twin, true and received signal phases, and
CARLA frames.

### 3.6 Ablation and Sensitivity Studies

Table [2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 3.6 Ablation and Sensitivity Studies ‣ 3 Experimental Results ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications")
evaluates the contribution of each major pipeline component by removing
it individually and comparing the resulting performance with the full
system. The ablations test launch conditioning, height-aware blockage,
the ground-truth rollout, the feasibility gate, the scene planner, and
prompt reflection.

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
|  Component and metric |  | With | Without    |  Component and metric |  | With | Without |
| Ground-truth rollout |  |  |  | Height-aware blockage |  |  |  |
|  Alarms raised (112 live scenes) | $`\downarrow`$ | 1 | 60    |  Divergences (15 healthy scenes) | $`\downarrow`$ | 34 | 60 |
|  False alarms among them | $`\downarrow`$ | 0 | 59    |  In-range coverage, Town10 (%) | $`\uparrow`$ | 100.0 | 47.7 |
| Feasibility gate |  |  |  | Scene planner (multi-approach junctions) |  |  |  |
|  IMA admissions per 150 executions | $`\uparrow`$ | 29.0 | 15.3    |  Conflict gap, ground-truth ego (m) | $`\downarrow`$ | 10.8 | 49.8 |
|  Seeds with zero admissions (of 3) | $`\downarrow`$ | 0 | 1    |  Conflict gap, message-driven ego (m) | $`\downarrow`$ | 2.4 | 5.7 |
| Launch conditioning |  |  |  | Prompt reflection |  |  |  |
|  Opening cross-track error, median (m) | $`\downarrow`$ | 0.06 | 1.22    |  Non-admitted prompts rescued (of 43) | $`\uparrow`$ | 8 | 0 |
|  Opening cross-track error, worst (m) | $`\downarrow`$ | 2.26 | 6.63    |  Scenes admitted beyond search reach | $`\uparrow`$ | 2 | 0 |
|  Spurious ground-truth collisions | $`\downarrow`$ | 0 | 1    |  |  |  |  |

Table 2: Ablation of LAST-V2X components. Each block removes one
component from the full pipeline; $`\uparrow`$/$`\downarrow`$ marks
whether a higher or lower value is better, and the better value is in
bold.

Several findings are notable. First, the ground-truth rollout is
essential for causal attribution. Among the 112 live scenes, 60 contain
at least one decision made under a divergent estimated state. A
divergence-only monitor would therefore raise 60 alarms, whereas the
paired rollout identifies only one communication-induced failure,
avoiding widespread false attribution. Second, the channel sensitivity
study shows that building blockage is the dominant communication
parameter. On Town10, reducing blockage loss from 5 to 1 dB/m increases
in-range road coverage from 47.7% to 95.8%, while changing transmit
power by $`\pm 10`$ dB shifts coverage by less than four percentage
points. Height-aware blockage also avoids the systematic
over-attenuation produced by a height-blind model. Third, the
feasibility gate and scene planner matter primarily when their
corresponding failure modes are present. Without the feasibility gate,
infeasible mutants enter the search and reduce IMA admissions from 29.0
to 15.3 per 150-execution ablation budget, averaged over three seeds,
while RLVW is largely unaffected because its mutations remain feasible.
Similarly, the scene planner has little effect on simple junctions but
becomes critical at multi-approach intersections, where heuristic
grounding can eliminate the intended conflict. Finally, prompt
reflection extends the refinement space beyond bounded parameter search.
It rescues eight non-admitted prompts, including two cases that search
alone cannot reach. When refinement is unsuccessful, reflection does not
force an admission; instead, it identifies why the scenario remains
ineffective or non-attributable.

## 4 Conclusion

This paper presented LAST-V2X, a language-driven, adaptive framework for
automated scenario synthesis and safety testing of vehicle-to-everything
(V2X) applications. By integrating large language models with domain
knowledge, physical traffic simulation, and communication modeling,
LAST-V2X transforms natural-language test descriptions into executable
scenarios that capture the interactions between vehicle behavior and V2X
information. Unlike conventional scenario-generation approaches that
primarily focus on physical traffic conditions, LAST-V2X explicitly
examines how communication degradation propagates through application
decisions to affect driving safety. A paired execution mechanism
distinguishes communication-induced failures from unsafe traffic
conditions, while execution-guided parameter search and LLM
self-reflection adaptively refine ineffective scenarios and identify
minimal reproducible failures.

Experiments across diverse CARLA environments and V2X safety
applications demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed framework.
LAST-V2X reliably generated executable scenarios from natural-language
descriptions while avoiding spurious failure attribution under healthy
communication. The paired execution mechanism further demonstrated the
importance of causal verification, as discrepancies between received
information and physical ground truth do not necessarily lead to unsafe
outcomes. Adaptive refinement substantially improved the discovery of
communication-induced failures by correcting ineffective fault
configurations and revising test descriptions based on simulation
evidence. Additional experiments highlighted how communication coverage,
information availability, and cooperation among connected vehicles
influence safety and driving behavior. Collectively, these findings
demonstrate the value of integrating language-driven scenario
generation, causal verification, and adaptive refinement into a unified
V2X testing framework.

Several limitations remain. First, the communication model and fault
configurations rely on representative parameters rather than
comprehensive measurements from real-world deployments. Second, the
evaluated safety applications employ simplified, deterministic decision
logic that may not fully capture the complexity of production V2X
systems. Third, although the main failure mechanisms were validated in
CARLA, large-scale adaptive search was conducted using a simplified
backend, and its effectiveness under fully integrated simulation remains
to be established. Finally, the current framework assumes fixed-time
traffic signals and does not explicitly distinguish communication errors
from changes in signal timing caused by adaptive traffic control.

Future research will focus on improving the realism, scalability, and
practical applicability of LAST-V2X. Integrating field-measured
communication characteristics and more advanced V2X application logic
will enable more representative evaluations of real-world connected
vehicle systems. Extending adaptive refinement to fully integrated CARLA
simulations and more complex traffic environments will further assess
the framework’s generalizability. Additional directions include
supporting actuated signal control, expanding the range of communication
and behavioral uncertainties, and using generated failure evidence to
inform communication infrastructure design and V2X safety improvements.
Ultimately, LAST-V2X provides a foundation for moving beyond manually
specified test cases toward automated, evidence-driven safety evaluation
of connected vehicle systems.

## Appendix A Verifier Check Families

The analytic verifier of Module I
(Section [2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Module I: LLM Agent Analysis ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications"))
screens every candidate specification before any simulator time is
spent. Each check is decidable from the specification and the
closed-form AoI relations alone, and returns a finding that names the
check, its severity, the specification fields responsible, and a minimal
repair, such as the breaching drop count $`k^{\ast}`$ of
Eq. ([16](#S2.E16 "In Analytic Feasibility Verification ‣ 2.2 Module I: LLM Agent Analysis ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications"))
or a minimum episode duration. Severity determines how a finding is
used:

- •
  Error findings are blocking. During intent parsing they are returned
  to the LLM parser, which revises the specification; during
  specification-space search
  (Section [2.5](#S2.SS5 "2.5 Module IV: Scenario Refinement ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications"))
  a mutant with any error finding is counted as gated and is never
  executed.
- •
  Warning findings do not block execution but mark a scenario whose
  outcome is unlikely to be attributable or informative, for example
  because the pristine channel already exceeds an age budget.
- •
  Note findings record a property of the scenario, such as a deliberate
  silent-miss probe in which every conflict agent is unequipped.

Verifier diagnostics also enter the evidence digest used by prompt-space
reflection.
Table [3](#A1.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Appendix A Verifier Check Families ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications")
lists the eleven check families. The conflict-timing check uses an
arrival-overlap window of 8 s, and the penetration check warns below a
market penetration rate of 0.2.

|  |  |
|----|----|
| Check |  Condition rejected or flagged |
| error blocking; returned to the parser for repair |  |
| no_effective_fault |  No fault can breach any application budget (a vacuous intent); suggestions name $`k^{\ast}`$ or a freeze/skew fault |
| anchor_beyond_horizon |  The $`k`$-th anchored occurrence, or the ego decision point, falls after the horizon $`T`$ |
| agent_unreachable |  The conflict cannot form |
| no_locus |  Retrieval returns no locus; the message names the first filter that empties the candidate set |
| warn executed, but flagged as unlikely to be attributable |  |
| fault_below_budget |  A particular fault is invisible to the safety criterion |
| baseline_blows_budget |  The pristine channel already exceeds a budget, so failures are not attributable to faults |
| conflict_timing_mismatch |  The arrival gap exceeds the overlap window |
| no_closing_speed |  The FCW/EEBL lead vehicle is not closing |
| mpr_low_unpinned |  Regimes mix under low market penetration |
| note recorded with the scenario |  |
| silent_miss_mode |  All conflict agents are pinned unequipped (structural probe) |
| outside_rsu_range_at_spawn |  Reception begins mid-approach |
````
