````math
## Appendix B Channel Model Details

Every V2I and V2V message passes independently through the spatial
channel of Module III
(Section [2.4](#S2.SS4 "2.4 Module III: Automated V2X Scenario Synthesis ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications"));
Table [4](#A2.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Latency and Delivery ‣ Appendix B Channel Model Details ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications")
lists its default parameters. For a transmitter–receiver pair at
distance $`d`$, the received signal strength of
Eq. ([24](#S2.E24 "In Spatial V2X Communication Channel ‣ 2.4 Module III: Automated V2X Scenario Synthesis ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications"))
is evaluated as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{RSSI}=\max\!\Big(P_{\mathrm{tx}}-10n\log_{10}\max(d,1\,\mathrm{m})-B_{\mathrm{blk}},\;P_{\mathrm{floor}}\Big),
``` |  | (29) |

and a link with $`d>R`$ is assigned the noise floor.

#### Height-Aware Blockage

The blockage term of
Eq. ([24](#S2.E24 "In Spatial V2X Communication Channel ‣ 2.4 Module III: Automated V2X Scenario Synthesis ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications"))
is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
B_{\mathrm{blk}}\;=\;\min\!\Big(\eta\!\int_{\mathrm{path}}\!\min\!\big(1,\,h_{\mathrm{exc}}(s)/h_{\mathrm{sat}}\big)\,ds,\;\;B_{\mathrm{NLOS}}\Big),
``` |  | (30) |

where
$`h_{\mathrm{exc}}(s)=\max\big(0,\,h_{\mathrm{b}}(s)-h_{\mathrm{ray}}(s)\big)`$
is the height by which the building at path position $`s`$ rises above
the sight line, and $`h_{\mathrm{ray}}(s)`$ falls linearly from the RSU
antenna height $`h_{\mathrm{RSU}}`$ to the receiver antenna height
$`h_{\mathrm{OBU}}`$. The integral is evaluated by sampling the ray at
steps of $`\Delta s`$. Loss therefore accrues only where a building
stands above the line of sight, grows with how far above it stands until
it saturates at $`h_{\mathrm{sat}}`$, and is capped at
$`B_{\mathrm{NLOS}}`$: however deep the obstruction, energy diffracted
over rooflines and reflected from facades still reaches the receiver.

#### Latency and Delivery

Latency grows linearly once the signal falls below a knee,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
L=L_{0}+\kappa\,\max\!\big(0,\;\mathrm{RSSI}_{\mathrm{knee}}-\mathrm{RSSI}\big),
``` |  | (31) |

and per-message delivery is logistic in RSSI,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
p_{\mathrm{del}}=\frac{1}{1+\exp\!\big((\mathrm{RSSI}_{50}-\mathrm{RSSI})/\nu\big)}.
``` |  | (32) |

Together,
Eqs. ([31](#A2.E31 "In Latency and Delivery ‣ Appendix B Channel Model Details ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications"))
and
([32](#A2.E32 "In Latency and Delivery ‣ Appendix B Channel Model Details ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications"))
realize the mapping $`g`$ of
Eq. ([24](#S2.E24 "In Spatial V2X Communication Channel ‣ 2.4 Module III: Automated V2X Scenario Synthesis ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications")).
A message is lost if its RSSI is at the noise floor or a Bernoulli draw
with probability $`1-p_{\mathrm{del}}`$ fails; otherwise it is delivered
after $`L`$. The semantic faults of Module III act on top of this
channel.

|  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|
|  Parameter | Symbol | Value    |  Parameter | Symbol | Value |
| Path loss |  |  | Height-aware blockage |  |  |
|  Transmit power | $`P_{\mathrm{tx}}`$ | 0 dBm    |  Building loss rate | $`\eta`$ | 5 dB/m |
|  Path-loss exponent | $`n`$ | 2.0    |  Ray sampling step | $`\Delta s`$ | 1 m |
|  Noise floor | $`P_{\mathrm{floor}}`$ | $`-100`$ dBm    |  RSU antenna height | $`h_{\mathrm{RSU}}`$ | 6.5 m |
|  Communication radius | $`R`$ | 100 m^(†)    |  Receiver antenna height | $`h_{\mathrm{OBU}}`$ | 1.5 m |
| Latency and delivery |  |  |  Saturation excess height | $`h_{\mathrm{sat}}`$ | 10 m |
|  Base latency | $`L_{0}`$ | 10 ms    |  NLOS loss cap | $`B_{\mathrm{NLOS}}`$ | 25 dB |
|  Latency slope | $`\kappa`$ | 0.2 ms/dB    | Message rates |  |  |
|  Latency knee | $`\mathrm{RSSI}_{\mathrm{knee}}`$ | $`-70`$ dBm    |  SPaT / MAP / BSM | $`1/T_{s}`$ | 10 / 1 / 10 Hz |
|  Delivery midpoint | $`\mathrm{RSSI}_{50}`$ | $`-90`$ dBm    |  |  |  |
|  Delivery scale | $`\nu`$ | 5 dB    |  |  |  |

Table 4: Default channel parameters. ^(†)The corridor study varies $`R`$
over 50, 100, and 150 m.

## Appendix C Fault Operators

Each fault is a typed primitive that states what is corrupted (the
target stream, SPaT, MAP, or BSM, and the field), when, and how much.
Its activation window is $`[t_{a}+o,\;t_{a}+o+\tau)`$, where $`t_{a}`$
is the time of the $`k`$-th occurrence of an anchor event, $`o`$ is an
offset that may be negative, and an unset duration $`\tau`$ keeps the
fault active until the scenario ends. The anchor events are sim_start,
green_onset, amber_onset, red_onset, phase_change,
ego_at_decision_point, and ego_enters_range; signal anchors resolve
against the bound signal group and kinematic anchors against the
message-driven ego. A fault may be restricted to one sender, and each
records the provenance of its magnitude (measured or representative);
the experiments in this paper use representative magnitudes.
Table [5](#A3.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Appendix C Fault Operators ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications")
defines the seven operators together with the parameter ranges explored
by specification-space search. Search additionally moves window offsets
in steps of $`\pm 2.5`$ s within $`[-10,10]`$ s, sets durations to
$`\{2,5,10\}`$ s or open, and changes the anchor event.

A freeze captures whatever the payload shows when its window opens. A
feed that should appear stuck at green is therefore anchored before the
amber onset (for example, amber_onset with an offset of $`-3`$ s or
earlier); a window anchored at red_onset captures yellow instead, and
the scenario typically stops safely.

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| Operator | Target |  Effect |  Search range |
| Delivery faults |  |  |  |
| drop | any |  Suppresses the next $`k`$ broadcasts in the window (all if $`k`$ is unset) |  $`k\in[1,40]`$ |
| burst_drop | any |  Gilbert–Elliott burst loss with transitions $`p_{\mathrm{gb}},p_{\mathrm{bg}}`$ and a bad-state loss rate |  pathology library |
| delay | any |  Constant delay plus jitter, optionally applied after reception (decode delay) |  $`[0.05,5]`$ s |
| Timestamp fault |  |  |  |
| skew | any |  Shifts the reported timestamp without delaying delivery, so the receiver misreads the age |  $`|\mathrm{skew}|\leq 30`$ s |
| Semantic-content faults |  |  |  |
| freeze | SPaT, BSM |  Holds phase, countdown, or kinematics at its value when the window opens |  window only |
| rebind | MAP |  Lanes of one movement report the signal group of another |  movement pair |
| pos_perturb | BSM |  Position noise $`\sigma`$ plus a constant along-track bias $`b`$ |  $`\sigma\in[0.2,10]`$ m, $`b\in[0,40]`$ m |

Table 5: Fault operators, their target streams, and the parameter ranges
explored by specification-space search.

## Appendix D Safety Application Logic

Each application is a deterministic kinematic-threshold function
$`\pi_{a}(\beta,x)`$
(Eq. ([2](#S2.E2 "In Physical and Perceived States ‣ 2.1 Problem Description ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications"))).
The same function drives both rollouts: the message-driven ego evaluates
it on the reconstructed state $`\beta`$ and the ground-truth ego on the
corresponding state derived from $`W`$, so any difference in their
outcomes is attributable to the information channel. Braking decisions
use a comfortable deceleration $`a_{c}=3.5`$ m/s² and a reaction time
$`t_{r}=1.0`$ s, giving the stopping distance

|     |                                         |     |      |
|-----|-----------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       d_{s}(v)=v\,t_{r}+\frac{v^{2}}{2a_{c}},
       ```                                      |     | (33) |

and the decision epoch of a signal application is the last point at
which stopping remains comfortable, $`d\leq d_{s}(v)`$, where $`d`$ is
the distance to the stop bar.
Table [6](#A4.T6 "Table 6 ‣ Appendix D Safety Application Logic ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications")
lists each decision rule and the violation that sets $`V=1`$ in
Eq. ([7](#S2.E7 "In Causal Failure Objective ‣ 2.1 Problem Description ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications")).

Violations are adjudicated identically for both rollouts. A red entry is
the crossing of the stop bar while the true signal of the ego’s group is
red; being beyond the bar when a later red begins is legal. A collision
requires a center-to-center distance below the stated threshold while
either vehicle moves faster than 0.5 m/s. For FCW and EEBL, only
vehicles ahead of the ego count, and the ego must be the striking
vehicle. In CARLA, a vehicle counts toward a conflict only if it lies
within 2.5 m of the ego’s route, so that adjacent-lane traffic passing
close to the ego is not scored as a crash.

The monitor that identifies divergence episodes uses the budgets of
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Safety Applications ‣ 3.1 Experiment Setup ‣ 3 Experimental Results ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications").
A signal belief is in error when its phase differs from the true phase
or its countdown differs by more than 1.0 s; a neighbor track is
displaced when its position error exceeds the position budget plus its
age multiplied by the vehicle’s speed; and a believed track whose
vehicle no longer exists becomes a ghost after 2.0 s.

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
| App. |  Decision rule |  Violation |
| Signal applications |  |  |
| RLVW |  Predicts the phase at arrival; once $`d\leq d_{s}(v)`$, stops if arrival falls on red, or on yellow after the countdown expires. Holds on a current red within 6 m of the bar; without signal data, stops at the decision point |  Red entry |
| GLOSA |  Keeps speed if arriving within the current green; otherwise advises $`v=d/t_{\mathrm{green}}`$, clipped to $`[3,16]`$ m/s |  Red entry |
| Conflict applications |  |  |
| IMA |  Stops if a crossing track reaches the conflict point within 3.5 s of the ego (ego arrival within 12 s) |  Collision, $`<1.8`$ m |
| LTA |  Stops if an opposing track arrives before the ego’s arrival plus a 4.0 s gap (12 s horizon) |  Collision, $`<1.8`$ m |
| FCW |  Brakes if the time to collision with the lead is below 2.5 s; holds behind a stopped lead within 10 m |  Forward collision, $`<2.0`$ m |
| EEBL |  Brakes on a relayed hard-braking flag from a lead vehicle within 80 m |  Forward collision, $`<2.0`$ m |

Table 6: Decision rules and violation criteria of the six safety
applications.

## Appendix E Failure Margin and Search Settings

The failure margin $`m(S)`$ of
Eq. ([9](#S2.E9 "In Causal Failure Objective ‣ 2.1 Problem Description ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications"))
measures how close an executed, non-admitted scenario came to failing;
smaller is closer. For signal applications it is the smallest
non-negative hazard slack over all divergence episodes,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
m(S)=\min_{e:\,\delta_{e}\geq 0}\delta_{e},\qquad\delta_{e}=\min_{t_{d}\in\mathcal{U}_{e}}\,(t_{d}-t^{\mathrm{end}}_{e}),
``` |  | (34) |

where $`\mathcal{U}_{e}`$ is the set of decision epochs $`t_{d}`$ of the
message-driven rollout that occur after episode $`e`$ begins, and
$`t^{\mathrm{end}}_{e}`$ is the episode’s end. A small slack means the
wrong belief ended just before a decision; a negative slack means a
decision was taken while the belief was wrong. For conflict
applications, $`m(S)`$ is the minimum distance between the
message-driven ego and any agent over the run, counting only vehicles
ahead of the ego for FCW and EEBL. If no episode has non-negative slack
(including a run without episodes) or no conflict occurs, $`m(S)`$ is
set to a large constant; a run whose episodes all have negative slack
therefore keeps this constant.

Specification-space search starts from the compiled scenario and keeps
an elite set of the $`K=8`$ highest-priority executed scenarios. Each
iteration samples a parent with probability proportional to $`w(S)`$
(Eq. ([26](#S2.E26 "In Specification-Space Search ‣ 2.5 Module IV: Scenario Refinement ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications")));
a scenario in which both rollouts violate is non-attributable and
receives the fixed priority 0.05 instead, the weight of a scenario with
$`m(S)=19.5`$, so it remains a possible parent but ranks below every
closer near miss. One of the operators in
Table [7](#A5.T7 "Table 7 ‣ Appendix E Failure Margin and Search Settings ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications")
is drawn, with weights that favor interaction-timing operators for
conflict applications and fault operators for signal applications.
Mutations never change the application, ego maneuver, agent roster, or
map query, so the test intent is preserved. Each mutant passes through
the verifier before execution, and the budget of $`N_{s}=120`$
candidates per scenario counts both executed and gated mutants. Admitted
scenarios remain in the elite set so that search can explore neighboring
mechanism cells. Each admitted scenario is minimized by delta debugging
(Section [2.5](#S2.SS5 "2.5 Module IV: Scenario Refinement ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications")).
The refinement study runs search with a fixed random seed on the stub
backend, and allows up to $`N_{r}=5`$ reflection rounds per scenario.

|  |  |
|----|----|
|  Operator |  Change |
| Fault vector |  |
|  Fault magnitude |  Scales a delay or skew by $`\times 0.5`$ or $`\times 2`$; changes a drop count by $`-5`$ to $`+10`$; scales $`\sigma`$ or shifts $`b`$ |
|  Fault window |  Shifts the offset by $`\pm 2.5`$ s, resets the duration, or changes the anchor event |
|  Stuck feed^(∗) |  SPaT phase and countdown freeze opening 2.5 or 5 s before the amber onset |
|  Outage^(∗) |  Window-long drop of the consumed stream (5, 8, or 12 s) |
|  Track freeze^(∗) |  Freezes neighbors’ BSM kinematics from 3–8 s before the ego’s decision point |
|  Position bias^(∗) |  Persistent BSM bias of 8, 15, or 25 m ($`\sigma=0.5`$ m) |
|  Pathology swap^(∗) |  Library pathology at a random intensity |
| Interaction and equipage |  |
|  Conflict alignment |  Places a conflict agent so that it arrives with the ego, to within $`\pm 8\%`$ |
|  Agent kinematics |  Shifts an agent’s distance by 5–40 m within $`[5,300]`$ m, or its speed by 0.5–3 m/s within $`[0.5,35]`$ m/s |
|  Ego speed |  Shifts the approach speed by $`\pm 2`$ m/s within $`[2,25]`$ m/s |
|  Penetration |  Shifts the market penetration rate by $`\pm 0.25`$ within $`[0,1]`$ |
|  SPaT rate |  Halves or doubles the SPaT rate within $`[1,20]`$ Hz |

Table 7: Mutation operators of specification-space search. ^(∗)Replaces
the scenario’s fault vector.

## Appendix F LLM Prompts

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 8: Condensed system prompts of the three LLM roles of LAST-V2X.

LAST-V2X uses three LLM roles that share one backend, GPT-4o at
temperature 0.2 with a fixed sampling seed
(Section [3](#S3 "3 Experimental Results ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications")).
Each receives a fixed system prompt, condensed in
Fig. [8](#A6.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ Appendix F LLM Prompts ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications"),
and must return a single JSON object that is validated before use. Rules
are paraphrased, and the worked examples in the parser prompt are
omitted. The domain notes given to the reflection role come from the V2X
knowledge base and are identical for every scenario; they are not tuned
to individual prompts.

## Appendix G Reproducibility

Table [8](#A7.T8 "Table 8 ‣ Appendix G Reproducibility ‣ LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications")
summarizes the configuration of each experiment. All runs are
deterministic given a scenario seed, which fixes vehicle equipage,
message-bus jitter, fault stochasticity, RSU pole selection, vehicle
blueprints, and retrieval tie-breaking, so every scene replays
identically. Each admitted failure is stored with its full
minimal-witness specification and re-verified against the paired
admission test on replay. For every benchmark scene, LAST-V2X archives
the compiled specification, the scene plan with its rationale, the
grounding record, the execution trace, the monitor report, three camera
streams with rendered V2I/V2V links, and RSSI, latency, and delivery
maps. Further material is available on the project page:
[https://keshuw95.github.io/LAST-V2X/](https://keshuw95.github.io/LAST-V2X/).

|  Experiment |  Scale | Seeds |

|  Communication-fault suite |  12 prompts | 1 per scene |
|  Corridor traversal |  6 prompts, Town05; 3 offset plans $`\times`$ 3 radio ranges | 10 (420 runs) |
|  Multiple connected vehicles |  6 prompts, Town05 | 10 per condition |
|  Refinement suite^(‡) |  50 prompts; $`\leq`$120 search candidates and $`\leq`$5 reflection rounds per scene | 1 per scene |
````
